posts.title: Leadership by Self Differentiation
posts.body:
A friend of mine, Jim Johnson, introduced me to the work of Edwin Friedman several years ago. It's one of those ideas I keep returning to because it explains something I've seen over and over in leaders who last and leaders who don't.

The concept is self-differentiation. And it has nothing to do with being cold or disconnected.

Friedman built his framework on the observation that emotional systems are contagious. The anxiety, reactivity, and mood of a group don't stay put; they spread (we are energetic beings after all). They look for hosts. They triangulate. Two people in conflict will almost always pull in a third party to attempt to stabilize the tension, and that third party, if they're not careful, absorbs the anxiety and becomes part of the system rather than a steady presence above it.

The self-differentiated leader is the one who can stay in the room without getting absorbed.

That's harder than it sounds. Most of us have been trained (by family systems, by organizations, by our own instincts) to calm the room by adjusting ourselves to the room. Someone's upset, so we soften. Someone pushes back, so we hedge. Someone needs us to be the villain of their story, so we unconsciously start playing the part. We mistake emotional reactivity for responsiveness and accommodation for leadership.

Self-differentiation doesn't mean you stop caring. It means you know who you are well enough that the pull of the system doesn't override it.

The leader who is differentiated can hold a clear position while staying genuinely connected to the people who disagree with it. Can tolerate the discomfort of someone's disappointment without rushing to make it go away. Can name what's happening in a relationship triangle without taking a side in it. This is not emotional distance. It's emotional maturity.

What I've found is that the biggest threat to this isn't bad people or even bad situations. It's the accumulated weight of small accommodations. You adjust here. You soften there. You avoid one more hard conversation. Over time, you've drifted far enough from your own center of gravity that you're not sure what you actually think anymore. You've become a reflection of everyone else's expectations rather than the expression of your best self.

Friedman called this being a "non-anxious presence." I think of it as knowing the difference between what you feel and what you are. The anxiety, the frustration, the pull to fix things; you can feel all of that without being governed by it. As my friend likes to quote at me, "Says easy. Does hard."

So where in your own world have you been adjusting yourself to calm the room?

posts.title: What Happens When You Stop
posts.body:
Four times a year, I go somewhere by myself and I don't come back until I've had enough quiet to actually think.

I block three days minimum. I leave the office behind. I don't call it a vacation because it isn't one. I call it a retreat because that's what it is: a deliberate withdrawal from the noise so something useful can surface. (I'm not the only one, by the way. Stacker CEO Noah Greenberg takes a silent three-day retreat every year.)

Most people I know have never done this. Most people I know are also operating at some level of perpetual low-grade overwhelm and can't figure out why their thinking feels shallow.

These two things are related.

Here's what I've noticed about busyness: it creates a very convincing illusion of progress...and everyone seems to constantly be "busy" (next time you ask someone how they're doing, notice how many people say "busy"). Calendar full, inbox pinging, back-to-back conversations; it all feels like doing. And some of it is. But the stuff that requires actual judgment, the hard questions about direction, the decisions you keep almost making, the things you know aren't right but haven't addressed; those don't get handled in the noise. They get deferred.

The retreat is where deferred things land.

The first day is always weird. There's a period of withdrawal from the pace. Your brain keeps reaching for the phone or the laptop, for the next task, for something to react to. I keep thinking of the other things that I could be focused on. If you let it settle, something shifts on day two. The thoughts you've been outrunning catch up. The clarity you've been hoping to find in the next book or the next conversation or the next planning session shows up when there's finally room for it.

I plan mine annually, but one per quarter. Not because I cracked some productivity code, but because I found that four months without one is long enough to lose the thread. Long enough to forget what matters versus what's urgent. Long enough to stop being the author of your own direction and start just responding to everyone else's.

The thing nobody tells you is that the hardest part isn't the time. Most people can find three days if they decide it matters and plan for it. The hardest part is deciding it matters before you feel like you deserve a break (or feeling like you "deserve" anything, if I'm honest).

You don't wait until you're depleted to eat. Solitude as a leadership practice works the same way. It's not recovery from the work. It's part of the work.

The question is whether it's on your calendar before someone else fills that slot. Because it will get filled. Something always will.

posts.title: Goals Don't Change You
posts.body:
Most goal-setting advice assumes the goal is the problem. Set a better goal. Make it more specific. Tie a deadline to it. Track it weekly. Is it a SMART goal?

That's not the problem.

The problem is that a goal is a target, not a transformation. And no matter how well-designed the target, hitting it (or missing it) doesn't change the operating system you're running on.

This is why you've watched people achieve big things and feel nothing. Crossed the finish line and immediately wondered what's next, as if the achievement didn't quite land. That's not ingratitude. That's what happens when the goal was never connected to identity in the first place.

Research out of TU Darmstadt found something that should bother every high-performer: when people set ambitious, specific goals and fall short (which is most of the time), their performance in the next cycle is worse, not better. The goal didn't motivate them. It marked them. And the mark carried forward.

Goals run on motivation. Motivation is finite. It spikes when the goal is new, fades as the novelty wears off, and collapses entirely when life gets hard or the gap feels too large. This is not a personal failing; it's how motivation works.

Identity is a different mechanism.

When you shift from "I want to run a marathon" to "I am someone who runs," you've stopped trying to reach a destination and started living from a description. Every run is a vote for who you are, not a step toward who you're trying to become. That's a different relationship to the behavior, and it's self-reinforcing in a way that goal-setting simply isn't.

This isn't about lowering the bar. It's about changing which direction you're pointed. Outcome goals ask what you want to achieve. Identity-based thinking asks who you are becoming. The second question is harder to dodge. You can defer a goal indefinitely by adjusting the timeline. You can't defer identity (you're either living it or you're not).

The goal you keep not hitting might not be a motivation problem. It might be that you've never actually decided to be the person who does it.

What would it look like to stop chasing that thing and just become the version of yourself who does it by default?

posts.title: Your January Goals Are a Procrastination Ritual
posts.body:
Every January, smart people sit down and write goals. They make them specific. They make them measurable. They attach timelines. Then they email them to their teams (or post them on a wall) and feel the quiet satisfaction of having done something. Then they blow them in short order (this is usually why I will skip the gym for the first half of January to avoid the crowds).

What they've actually done is defer a decision.

A goal is a statement about a future version of yourself. "I will grow revenue 40% this year." "I will get into better shape." "I will spend more time with my family." These are descriptions of what you hope to be true someday. They require no present action. They are deniable until December (or whenever). And if they don't happen, you can always reset next January.

A decision is different. A decision is irreversible (or at least, reversing it has a cost you have to own). "We don't take clients under $500K" is not a goal. It's a constraint you operate inside right now. "I don't eat junk food" is not a goal. It's a description of how you live. The present tense matters. The commitment structure is entirely different.

Researchers Schweitzer and Ordonez spent years studying what actually happens when people and organizations set ambitious specific goals. The findings weren't flattering. Narrow goals create tunnel vision. People hit the metric and miss everything adjacent to it. When falling short feels like failure, a meaningful percentage of people don't try harder. They adjust the numbers. They rationalize. The goal doesn't push them toward integrity. It pushes them toward self-deception.

This isn't an argument against aspiration (I'm all for aspirations and having long-term vision and goals). It's an argument against confusing a goal with a commitment.

The leaders I've seen build things that last are not the most disciplined goal-setters. They're the most committed decision-makers. They've made a small number of clear, present-tense choices about how they operate, what they're willing to do, and what they're not; and those choices hold even when motivation is low, even when the quarter is hard, even when no one is watching. They're also easier to pick up when you have that one drop. Just start again with another decision.

Goals are easy to write and easy to forget. Decisions are harder to make precisely because they mean something.

So what are you calling a goal this year that's really a decision you haven't made yet?
